facts.title: Discovered Twice Over
facts.text: Actinium was first isolated in 1899 by French chemist André-Louis Debierne, a close colleague of Marie and Pierre Curie, from residues of uranium ore. Just three years later, in 1902, German chemist Friedrich Oskar Giesel independently rediscovered it and proposed the name 'emanium.' The name 'actinium' won out, derived from the Greek word 'aktis,' meaning ray or beam.

facts.title: It Literally Glows in the Dark
facts.text: Actinium is so intensely radioactive that it makes the surrounding air glow with an eerie pale-blue light. This happens because its emitted radiation excites nitrogen and oxygen molecules in the air, which then release the absorbed energy as visible light. The effect is similar in cause to the blue glow seen in nuclear reactor pools.

facts.title: Named the Whole Family
facts.text: Actinium gives its name to the entire actinide series, the 15 elements running from actinium (Z=89) through lawrencium (Z=103). This group includes famous elements like uranium and plutonium, all of which share similar electron-filling behavior in the 5f subshell. Sitting at the head of the row, actinium is the namesake template for this part of the periodic table.

facts.title: Vanishingly Rare on Earth
facts.text: Natural actinium is incredibly scarce, occurring only as a fleeting decay product of uranium and thorium in their ores. A ton of uranium ore contains only about 0.2 milligrams of actinium-227. Because of this extreme rarity, almost all actinium used in research and medicine is produced artificially in reactors or accelerators.

facts.title: A Promising Cancer Fighter
facts.text: Actinium-225 is one of the most exciting isotopes in modern targeted alpha-particle cancer therapy. Attached to molecules that home in on tumor cells, it delivers a burst of alpha radiation that destroys cancer over a very short range while sparing nearby healthy tissue. Clinical studies, especially for prostate cancer, have shown striking results, fueling a global effort to produce more of this scarce isotope.

facts.title: The 21-Year Clock
facts.text: The most stable and commonly studied isotope, actinium-227, has a half-life of about 21.8 years. Other isotopes are far more fleeting: actinium-225 lasts only about 10 days, while many others decay in minutes or seconds. No isotope of actinium is stable, so every atom of it is steadily transforming into other elements.

facts.title: Hotter Than You'd Expect
facts.text: A sample of actinium-227 is warm to the touch because its radioactive decay continuously releases energy as heat. The element is roughly 150 times more radioactive than radium of the same mass, making even tiny quantities require careful shielding and remote handling. This self-heating is a direct, tangible demonstration of nuclear energy at work.

facts.title: A Silvery, Reactive Metal
facts.text: In pure form, actinium is a soft, silvery-white metal that tarnishes quickly when exposed to air. It reacts with oxygen and moisture, forming a white coating of actinium oxide that actually helps protect the metal underneath from further corrosion. Its melting point is around 1,050 degrees Celsius, and chemically it behaves much like its lighter cousin, lanthanum.

facts.title: No Job in Living Things
facts.text: Actinium has no known biological role and is not needed by any living organism. If it enters the body, it tends to accumulate in the liver and especially the bones, where its alpha radiation can damage tissue over time. For this reason it is considered a serious radiological hazard rather than a nutrient or trace element.

facts.title: A Standard Candle for Tools
facts.text: Because actinium-227 decays in a well-characterized chain that includes a steady production of helium and other daughter products, it has been used as a neutron source when mixed with beryllium. These actinium-beryllium sources can be useful for instrument calibration and certain types of radiography. Researchers also value pure actinium-227 as a way to generate small, controlled amounts of its medically prized descendant, actinium-225.
